body.heading: How the list works
paragraphs: When you feel the urge to buy something you had not planned to buy, do not buy it — write it down instead. Note the item, the price, and today's date, then wait thirty full days. If you still want it after the wait, and it fits your budget, buy it without guilt. If the urge has faded, you have just saved the money and avoided the regret.

The wait works because impulse buying is usually emotional: boredom, stress, a sale countdown, a post on social media. Thirty days gives that feeling time to fade, so the decision is made by your calmer self. One consumer survey put the average American's impulse spending at about $150 a month — over $1,800 a year — so even catching half of those urges adds up to real money.

The rule is only for non-essential purchases: clothes, gadgets, homeware, entertainment. Groceries, medicine, and urgent repairs are exempt, and for a small purchase a shorter wait — a day, or a week — is often enough.

body.heading: Set your threshold
paragraphs: Pick a price above which the rule applies. Many people start at $50 or $100 and adjust to fit their income. Below the threshold, a 24-hour pause is usually enough; above it, the full thirty days earns its keep.

Keep the list somewhere you will actually see it — a note on your phone, or a page on the fridge. Add a calendar reminder for day thirty. When the reminder arrives, compare prices across a couple of shops before you buy; you may find the same item cheaper, or realise the wanting has quietly gone. Either way, the list has done its job: the purchase, if it happens, is a choice, not a reflex.

takeaway: Waiting thirty days turns an impulse into a decision — and most impulses do not survive the wait.
